detail: supported
This process lifts 2D observations into a consistent 3D representation [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the process lifts 2D observations into a consistent 3D representation. The evidence explicitly mentions 'Uplifting 2D Semantics into 3D Feature Fields' and describes how the method predicts per-point feature signals (f) in 3D space which are then supervised by reprojecting them onto the 2D image plane. The text also notes that this yields 'spatially consistent and invariant semantics'. Therefore, the core assertion of the claim is directly supported by the provided text.
supported

Augmented features are computed by sampling from high-resolution 2D image features (typically $160 \times 120$) instead of low-resolution volume features ($40 \times 40 \times 16$) to address aliasing [S4].

The claim states that augmented features are computed by sampling from high-resolution 2D image features (typically 160x120) instead of low-resolution volume features (40x40x16) to address aliasing. The evidence in Source [S4] explicitly states: 'In 3D detection, we use a lower grid resolution of 40 × 40 × 16, which suffers from the aliasing issue... To mitigate this, we draw inspiration from [44, 53] and sample features from higher resolution 2D image feature maps, typically of size 160 × 120'. It further confirms that 'we sample point features along the ray from the multi-view image features instead of the low-resolution volume features' and that this approach yields better performance. All specific details in the claim are present and supported by the text.
supported
A function $f(\mathbf{p})$ that maps a 3D point $\mathbf{p}$ to an object code vector $\mathbf{o}$, representing object ownership independent of viewing angles [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that a function $f( oldsymbol{p})$ maps a 3D point $ oldsymbol{p}$ to an object code vector $ oldsymbol{o}$ representing object ownership independent of viewing angles. Source [S2] explicitly defines the object field as a function of coordinates because the object signature is 'irrelevant to the viewing angles' (independent of viewing angles). It further states that the object code $ oldsymbol{o}$ aims to 'accurately describe the object ownership' and formally defines $ oldsymbol{o} = f( oldsymbol{p})$. All components of the claim are present in the evidence.
supported

Semantic-NeRF was the first to introduce semantic fields within the NeRF framework, using ground-truth semantic segmentation maps to augment the radiance field with per-point semantic logits [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that Semantic-NeRF was the first to introduce semantic fields within the NeRF framework and used ground-truth semantic segmentation maps to augment the radiance field with per-point semantic logits. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in the passage: 'Semantic-NeRF [207], notably, was the first to introduce semantic fields within the NeRF framework. Using ground-truth semantic segmentation maps, it augments the radiance field with per-point semantic logits...' All facts in the claim are present in the evidence.
supported
Supervision is performed by comparing the rendered feature $\hat{\mathbf{F}}(r)$ against ground-truth 2D feature maps or teacher network outputs projected onto the image plane [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that supervision involves comparing rendered features against ground-truth 2D feature maps or teacher network outputs projected onto the image plane. The evidence in Source [S1] explicitly states: 'Supervision is achieved by reprojecting the predicted features onto the image plane and comparing them to their corresponding 2D feature maps'. It also mentions that these features can encode '2D Foundation Models embeddings', which aligns with the 'teacher network outputs' part of the claim. Therefore, all facts in the claim are supported by the evidence.
supported

Feature Fields generalize the standard Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) formulation by predicting arbitrary per-point feature signals $\mathbf{f}$ in addition to volume density $\sigma$ and color $\mathbf{c}$ [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that Feature Fields generalize the standard NeRF formulation by predicting arbitrary per-point feature signals f in addition to volume density σ and color c. Source [S1] explicitly confirms this in the passages, stating: 'feature fields generalize the NeRF formulation to predict arbitrary per-point feature signals rather than only color' and showing the formal extension from FΘ(x, d) -> (c, σ) to FΘ(x, d) -> (f, c, σ). The notes also corroborate this definition.
supported
The function $f$ is parameterized by a series of MLPs [S2, unofficial].

The claim states that the function f is parameterized by a series of MLPs. The provided evidence from Source [S2] explicitly states in the notes and the main text: 'The function f is parameterized by a series of MLPs.' Therefore, every fact in the claim is directly supported by the evidence.
supported
Samples point features along the ray from multi-view image features instead of low-resolution volume features to address the need for high-resolution images in NeRF [S4].

The claim states that samples point features along the ray from multi-view image features instead of low-resolution volume features to address the need for high-resolution images in NeRF. The evidence in Source [S4] explicitly confirms this in Section 3.2 ('Feature Sampling'), stating that previous NeRFs sample from high-resolution 3D volumes, but this method uses a lower grid resolution which suffers from aliasing. To mitigate this, they sample from higher resolution 2D image feature maps. Section 4 also reiterates: 'we sample point features along the ray from the multi-view image features instead of the low-resolution volume features.' Thus, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported

Density and latent features are computed as $\sigma(\mathbf{p}), \hat{\mathbf{h}}(\mathbf{p}) = \text{G-MLP}(\bar{V}(\mathbf{p}), \gamma(\mathbf{p}))$, and color as $\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{d}) = \text{C-MLP}(\hat{\mathbf{h}}(\mathbf{p}), \mathbf{d})$ [S4].

The claim states that density and latent features are computed as $σ(p), ĥ(p) = G-MLP(V̄(p), γ(p))$ and color as $c(p, d) = C-MLP(ĥ(p), d)$. Source [S4] explicitly provides these exact equations in Section 3.2 (Equation 4) and defines the variables consistently with the claim (V̄(p) as augmented ray features, γ(p) as position encoding, ĥ as latent features). Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported
Points are sampled along the ray $\mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t \times \mathbf{d}$ [S4].

The claim states that points are sampled along the ray defined by the equation r(t) = o + t * d. Source [S4] explicitly states in Section 3.2: 'Specifically, we first sample points along the ray originated from the camera, i.e., r(t) = o + t × d where o is the ray origin and d is the view direction.' This matches the claim exactly.
supported
Subsequent works have extended this to include physical properties, latent descriptors from 2D foundation models, and object codes [S1, unofficial][S2, unofficial][S3].

The claim states that subsequent works extend the formulation to include 'physical properties', 'latent descriptors from 2D foundation models', and 'object codes'. Source [S1] explicitly confirms that the feature field formulation can encode 'physical properties (e.g. temperature, sound, magnetic waves, ...)' and 'any other latent descriptor (e.g. 2D Foundation Models embeddings)'. Source [S2] explicitly describes 'Object Fields' that predict an 'object code vector o' representing object ownership. Therefore, all specific items mentioned in the claim are present in the provided evidence.
supported

Additionally, the notes section reiterates: 'Augmented feature V̄ is a concatenation of {V_avg, V_var, RGB_avg, RGB_var}.' All components mentioned in the claim are present and correctly described in the evidence.

The core mechanism modifies the radiance field function $F_\Theta$ to map input coordinates $(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d})$ to a tuple $(\mathbf{f}, \mathbf{c}, \sigma)$, where $\mathbf{f} \in \mathbb{R}^d$ is a feature vector [S1, unofficial].

The claim states that the core mechanism modifies the radiance field function $F_Θ$ to map input coordinates $(x, d)$ to a tuple $(f, c, σ)$, where $f$ is a feature vector. Source [S1] explicitly provides the formal mapping $F_Θ (x, d) → (f, c, σ)$ and defines $f ∈ R^d$ as a vector representing feature signals. Therefore, every fact in the claim is present in the evidence.
supported

Augments sampled features with variance from multiple views to describe occupancy: low variance implies occupied 3D location (Lambertian assumption), while high variance implies free space (different appearances from different views) [S4].

The claim is fully supported by the text in Source [S4]. The text explicitly states: 'we augment the sampled features with the variance from multiple views... The variance of the color features is able to roughly describe the occupancy of the 3D field... If the 3D location p is occupied, the variance of the observed features should be low under the assumption that the scene only contains Lambertian surfaces. On the other hand, if the location is in free space, different appearances would be observed from different views, and therefore the variance of color features would be high.' This matches every component of the claim.
supported
This approach achieves 20.51 PSNR for novel-view synthesis compared to 18.93 with volume sampling [S4].

The claim states that the approach achieves 20.51 PSNR for novel-view synthesis compared to 18.93 with volume sampling. Source [S4] explicitly states in the text: 'For the novel-view synthesis task using NeRF branch, sampling from image features achieves 20.51 in PSNR comparing to 18.93 with volume sampling.' This matches the claim exactly.
